Topology The initial design of subcomponent consists of triangular lattice as shown in Fig. 4.3.3. When overmolded 16 | P age the polymer composite will be separated into the different triangular islands formed by the struts of the triangular lattice. Thus, the reinforcing effect of the polymer is limited. To overcome this, the struts are modified to provide passage in between them interconnecting the overmolded polymer composite throughout, as shown in Design 1 of Fig. 4.3.3. Furthermore, the interface between the polymer composite and metal bracket is a region of high stress concentration and is susceptible for crack initiation and failure. To avoid this, the design if further modified to extend the metal bracket at the interface on either side of the subcomponent. Figure 4.3.2. The optimized design obtained after the above iterations is analyzed for a static load of 100 N as shown in Fig. 4.3.4. The subcomponent design is compared with the original Ford’s subcomponent design along with their resultant displacement contours in Fig. 4.3.4. The optimized subcomponent weighs 0.96 kg as compared to original subcomponent weight of 1.68 kg and thus enables significant weight saving. The comparison of resultant displacement contours also reveal that the maximum displacement of the polymer-based subcomponent is significantly smaller than the original design. Thus, the designed subcomponent is lightweight while satisfying the mechanical performance requirements. Figure 4.3.3. The optimized subcomponent is assembled into the entire polymer composite seatback frame as described in Section 4.4. To ensure that the polymer-based seatback design is lightweight as compared to the original seatback frame, the polymer-based seatback along with the subcomponent are iteratively re- designed. However, the subcomponent design obtained in this section is used as reference and is very similar to the final subcomponent that is assembled into the entire seatback, as discussed in Section 4.4. 4.4 Seatback Frame Design In this section, the design of entire seatback by combining the metal and polymer composite through AM-CM process is detailed. The original Ford’s seatback frame is shown in Fig. 4.4.1 (a) with the boundary conditions in Fig. 4.4.1 (b). A contour of the resultant displacement for the applied load of 3 kN and boundary conditions is shown in Fig. 4.4.1(c). The entire seatback frame is optimized through multiple iterations to make it lightweight using a combination of metal parts overmolded with polymer composites. The seatback frame design evolving through multiple iterations are shown in Fig. 4.4.2. Both the metal and polymer composites area are improved in subsequent design iterations to enable the low weight and high mechanical performance requirement.
